content: Loxoprofen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that belongs to the propionic acid derivatives group, which also includes drugs like ibuprofen and naproxen. It is marketed under the trade name Loxonin in countries such as Brazil, Mexico, and Japan, where it is available as its sodium salt form, loxoprofen sodium. In Argentina, it is sold under the name Oxeno. Loxoprofen is primarily available for oral administration in these regions, and a transdermal formulation was approved for use in Japan in January 2006. Loxoprofen is classified as a prodrug, meaning it is pharmacologically inactive until it is metabolized in the body. After oral administration, it is rapidly converted into its active metabolite, a trans-alcohol derivative. This active form reaches its peak plasma concentration within 30 to 50 minutes after ingestion. The mechanism of action of loxoprofen is similar to that of most NSAIDs. It acts as a non-selective inhibitor of cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, thereby reducing the production of prostaglandins from arachidonic acid. Prostaglandins are mediators of inflammation, pain, and fever, and their inhibition accounts for the drug's anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects. Loxoprofen should not be used concurrently with second-generation quinolone antibiotics, such as ciprofloxacin and norfloxacin, because this combination can enhance the inhibition of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) activity, potentially leading to seizures. Additionally, loxoprofen may increase the plasma concentrations of certain drugs, including warfarin, methotrexate, sulfonylurea derivatives, and lithium salts. Therefore, caution is advised when administering loxoprofen to patients who are taking any of these medications, as the risk of adverse effects or toxicity may be heightened.
